snip.t: Severe pneumonia is reserved for danger signs such as inability to drink, convulsions, lethargy or stridor, and needs referral and injectable treatment.
Ceftriaxone: Third-generation cephalosporin — Severe pneumonia (IV) — Biliary sludge, allergy
Timing matters: in severe pneumonia give the first antibiotic dose within 4 hours (sooner in sepsis), and take blood cultures first if this does not delay treatment.

qs.q: A 48‑year‑old patient with severe pneumonia receives high‑flow oxygen but his PaO₂ remains low. Which mechanism most likely limits the benefit of supplemental oxygen?
qs.e: In a true shunt, blood bypasses ventilated alveoli, so oxygen therapy has little effect. Diffusion impairment and V/Q mismatches still allow some improvement with supplemental oxygen.
qs.s: Respiratory System: Airways, Lung Diseases and Chest X-ray: MCQs

qs.q: An alcoholic patient develops a severe pneumonia producing thick, mucoid 'currant jelly' sputum. The isolated Gram-negative opportunistic rod owes its prominent mucoid colonial appearance and resistance to phagocytosis primarily to which surface component?
o: A thick peptidoglycan shell reinforced with teichoic acids
A dense network of surface fimbriae and pili appendages
A repeating O-antigen side chain on outer membrane lipids
A heavily mycolated outer lipid envelope structure
An extensive, hyperviscous polysaccharide capsule layer
qs.e: Klebsiella pneumoniae produces a prominent polysaccharide capsule that confers a mucoid phenotype and protects against phagocytosis.
qs.s: Weekly Year 2: Microbiology Exam - November 6, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: An immunocompromised patient develops severe pneumonia. A diagnostic sputum Gram stain reveals encapsulated, lancet-shaped Gram-positive diplococci. Which virulence factor is primarily responsible for preventing opsonization and phagocytosis of this organism?
o: An IgA protease enzyme cleaving mucosal immunoglobulins
A surface protein A binding the Fc region of antibodies
A lipoteichoic acid layer projecting through peptidoglycan
A destructive pneumolysin pore-forming toxin molecule
A complex polysaccharide capsule surrounding the cell wall
qs.e: Streptococcus pneumoniae relies on its polysaccharide capsule to evade phagocytic clearance by inhibiting host opsonization.

qs.q: A middle-aged alcoholic patient presents with severe pneumonia and coughs up thick, gelatinous, blood-tinged sputum. A Gram-negative encapsulated rod is cultured on agar. What is the primary pathogenic mechanism of tissue destruction here?
qs.e: Klebsiella pneumoniae causes extensive hemorrhagic necrosis and cavitation driven by its massive polysaccharide capsule.

qs.q: A 55-year-old chronic alcoholic develops severe pneumonia with currant-jelly sputum. Gram-negative bacilli with a prominent mucoid capsule are isolated on MacConkey agar. The hypermucoid appearance is due to which structure?
o: Fimbrial adhesin array on outer surface
qs.e: Klebsiella pneumoniae produces a large polysaccharide capsule responsible for the classic mucoid colonies and currant-jelly sputum.

qs.q: A 28-year-old man is admitted with severe pneumonia and a parapneumonic effusion. Pleural fluid pH is 7.10 with high LDH and low glucose. What is the mandatory next step in the management of this patient?
o: Therapeutic thoracentesis removing no more than 1.5 litres
Insertion of a chest drain for complicated pleural infection
Initiation of oral broad-spectrum outpatient antibiotics alone
qs.e: A parapneumonic effusion with a pH below 7.20 indicates a complicated infection with bacterial invasion that will not resolve on antibiotics alone and requires a chest drain. Simple sterile effusions with a pH above 7.20 can be managed with antibiotics alone.
qs.s: Pleural Effusion: Light's Criteria, Fluid Analysis and Management: MCQs

qs.q: A 45-year-old man with severe pneumonia is admitted to the surgical ICU. His arterial blood gas demonstrates a low PaO2 and a high PaCO2. Which of the following conditions is most characteristically associated with this specific blood gas profile?
qs.e: A low PaO2 combined with a high PaCO2 defines Type II ventilatory or hypercapnic respiratory failure, for which COPD is a classic cause. Pulmonary embolism and ARDS typically present with Type I hypoxaemic respiratory failure with a normal or low PaCO2.
qs.s: Surgical Critical Care: ICU, Respiratory Failure, Ventilation, Blood: MCQs

qs.q: A 45-year-old chronic alcoholic presents with severe pneumonia, hemoptysis, and a thick gelatinous sputum that is described as red currant-jelly. Which causative pathogen is most consistent with these findings?
qs.e: Klebsiella infection is classically associated with alcoholism, diabetes, aspiration, and sputum characterized as red currant-jelly. Mycoplasma pneumoniae is an atypical organism typically presenting with a dry cough and nonexudative pharyngitis rather than red currant-jelly sputum.

es.q: A patient is admitted to the ICU with severe pneumonia and develops Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS). Describe the hallmark microscopic finding in the acute phase of ARDS and outline the crucial early pathogenic step involving cellular mediators.
es.m: The hallmark microscopic finding in the acute phase of ARDS is Diffuse Alveolar Damage (DAD), characterized by the presence of hyaline membranes. A crucial early pathogenic step involves pulmonary macrophages releasing IL-8, which acts as a potent chemoattractant for neutrophils.

ai.subject: Paediatrics
ai.summary: Severe pneumonia in children is a life‑threatening infection marked by danger signs such as chest indrawing, inability to drink, convulsions or severe lethargy. Rapid recognition, prompt injectable antibiotics and oxygen are essential to prevent death.

sections.p: Severe pneumonia is defined by WHO as pneumonia with any danger sign: chest indrawing, inability to drink, convulsions, severe lethargy, or stridor in a calm child. Diagnosis is clinical; chest X‑ray is supportive but not required in low‑resource settings.
b: Danger signs are the key diagnostic criteria

sections.p: WHO classifies pneumonia into no pneumonia, non‑severe, and severe. Severe pneumonia requires admission and injectable antibiotics. In resource‑rich settings, severity may be graded by oxygen saturation, respiratory rate, and need for ventilation.

Bacterial pathogens dominate: Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae type b, and Staphylococcus aureus. In low‑resource areas, HIV‑associated bacterial pneumonia, tuberculosis, and malaria‑related pulmonary complications are common. Viral causes (RSV, influenza) can precipitate bacterial superinfection.
Rapid onset of cough, tachypnea, and chest indrawing. The child may be irritable, have poor feeding, or be lethargic. Stridor indicates upper airway involvement. Oxygen saturation <90% is a red flag.
Investigations confirm diagnosis, guide therapy, and rule out mimics. In low‑resource settings, focus on simple, rapid tests.

t.b: Measures oxygen saturation; <90% indicates hypoxia and need for oxygen
Rules out malaria as cause of respiratory distress
Identifies bacterial pathogen; obtain before antibiotics if it does not delay treatment
Shows consolidation or effusion; useful if available but not mandatory
Leukocytosis or neutropenia may suggest bacterial infection; anemia can worsen hypoxia

sections.p: Severe sepsis, respiratory failure, pneumothorax, empyema, and septic shock are life‑threatening complications. Watch for worsening tachypnea, cyanosis, or altered consciousness.
Treat the underlying infection with injectable antibiotics, provide oxygen, and support hydration and nutrition. Choose antibiotics based on local resistance patterns and drug availability.
b: Injectable benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin is first‑line in WHO guidelines

t.b: Treats S. pneumoniae and H. influenzae; chosen for low cost and efficacy
Adds coverage for Gram‑negative organisms; avoid in renal impairment
Corrects hypoxia; use low‑flow nasal cannula if available
Maintain perfusion; avoid fluid overload in compromised lungs

sections.p: Discharge when afebrile for 48 h, breathing normal, and able to feed. Vaccination against pneumococcus and Hib, hand hygiene, and prompt treatment of cough in the community reduce incidence.
b: Vaccination is the cornerstone of prevention

sections.p: Bronchiolitis, asthma exacerbation, and pneumonia with pleural effusion can mimic severe pneumonia. Distinguish by history, clinical signs, and simple investigations.
b: Bronchiolitis presents with wheeze rather than chest indrawing

sections.p: Normal chest X‑ray does not exclude severe pneumonia; early consolidation may be missed. Pulse oximetry can be falsely normal if perfusion is poor. Blood cultures may be negative if antibiotics were given before sampling.
b: Early consolidation may be invisible on X‑ray

faq.q: Why is oxygen therapy essential in severe pneumonia?
faq.a: It corrects hypoxia, reduces work of breathing, and prevents organ failure.

faq.q: Can I use oral antibiotics for severe pneumonia?
faq.a: No; injectable antibiotics are required because oral absorption may be unreliable and the infection is life‑threatening.
Use amikacin or a third‑generation cephalosporin if local resistance patterns allow; monitor renal function.

exam: Explain why chest indrawing is a danger sign and how it guides treatment decisions.
Describe the first‑line injectable antibiotic regimen for severe pneumonia in a child with suspected bacterial etiology.
Outline the steps you would take if a child with severe pneumonia develops sudden worsening of breathing and cyanosis.
